questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the central claim of the passage?
options: Vivid memories are always more accurate than hazy ones because they are felt so strongly.
Human memory decays steadily with age until little of the original event remains.
Memory evolved as a perfect archive but has been corrupted by modern life.
Remembering is an act of reconstruction that alters the memory even as it recalls it.
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: We speak of memory as if it were a recording, faithfully stored and replayed on demand. The evidence points the other way. Each act of recollection is less a retrieval than a reconstruction, assembled afresh from fragments and, in the assembling, quietly altered. What we take to be a vivid memory of an event is often a memory of the last time we recalled it, with each retelling laying down a fresh version that overwrites the old. The confidence we feel bears no reliable relation to accuracy; the most vivid and certain memories are as prone to distortion as the hazy ones, and sometimes more so, for their very vividness discourages doubt. This is not a defect to be lamented so much as the price of a system built for use rather than for the archive. A memory that updated itself with every fresh experience served our ancestors better than a perfect but rigid record would have. The uncomfortable corollary, which the courts have been slow to absorb, is that sincerity is no guarantee of truth: a witness may be wholly honest and wholly mistaken at once, and no amount of certainty on the stand can close the gap between the two.

questions.stem: The two drivers are described primarily in order to:
options: expose a clash between how we claim to judge and how we really do
show that careless drivers are usually punished far too leniently by the courts
argue that luck plays no real part at all in questions of moral blame
prove that using a phone while driving should carry a much heavier penalty
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: Consider two drivers, equally careless, who each glance down at a phone for the same reckless instant. On the first driver's road a child happens to step out, and is killed; on the second's, the road happens to be empty, and nothing occurs. The law will treat these two very differently, and so, if we are honest, will we: the first we are inclined to call a killer, the second merely a fool who got away with it. Yet the only difference between them lies in something wholly outside their control — the presence or absence of a child neither could have foreseen. This is the puzzle philosophers have called moral luck. We like to believe that a person can be judged only for what lies within his will, and that the workings of chance should make no difference to praise or blame. Our actual practice flatly contradicts this comforting principle at every turn. We heap censure on the reckless driver who is unlucky and quietly forgive the one who is not, though their choices were identical. To resolve the tension we must give up one of two convictions we are each loath to surrender: either that we are answerable only for what we control, or that outcomes rightly bear on how harshly we are judged. The discomfort of the problem lies precisely in our reluctance to abandon either.

questions.subject: Cloze Passage
questions.passage: The gravest errors of judgement are rarely the work of stupidity; more often they are the (63)________ of intelligence pressed into the service of a conclusion already reached. A clever mind, having decided what it wishes to believe, is formidably resourceful in (64)________ reasons to believe it. It does not weigh the evidence so much as (65)________ it, admitting what flatters the favoured view and quietly discounting what does not. The layman imagines that expertise is a shield against this temptation; in truth it often (66)________ the danger, for the expert commands precisely the arguments needed to defend whatever he has already concluded. What protects a thinker is therefore not cleverness, which can be (67)________ to any cause, but a positively uncomfortable willingness to seek out the evidence that would prove him (68)________. Such a habit runs against every instinct we possess; we are built to defend our beliefs, not to (69)________ them. The rare individuals who master it are seldom the quickest in a room, but they are the ones whose conclusions, arrived at slowly and against their own inclination, tend in the long run to (70)________. They have learned the hardest of intellectual disciplines: to treat their own cherished opinion as the (71)________ most in need of cross-examination, and to feel a certain suspicion toward any idea that has cost them nothing to (72)________.
questions.direction: Select the most appropriate word for each blank in the passage.
